speaker: Siddhartha Mukherjee
title: The Alarming New Risks of Cancer Everyone Needs to Hear
question: In cancer biology, why is the classic model of genetic mutations alone no longer enough to explain how tumors start?
guest: This was a surprise from recent work done by many people. People used to think a cancer cell acquired genetic mutations, commandeered its genes, and off it went into a tumor. It turns out it's more complicated and chilling than that: there are lots and lots of sleeper cancer cells in everyone's body, in various organs, and they're just asleep—they're dormant, and they'll probably do nothing to you for the rest of your life. The new theory is that they need to be woken up, and at least one of those wake-up signals is chronic inflammation. So rather than one morning a cell suddenly acquiring genetic mutations and taking off into a nasty tumor, there are thousands of dormant mutated cells sitting in your body, and something happens in the internal environment—like chronic inflammation—that wakes them up. It still has to be validated further, but it fundamentally changes the paradigm of how we think about cancer.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The classic somatic mutation model holds that tumors arise when a cell accumulates enough driver mutations in oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes. That picture is now seen as incomplete, for several reasons.

First, deep sequencing of healthy tissues (skin, esophagus, blood, endometrium) shows that normal cells routinely carry classic driver mutations, such as in TP53, NOTCH1 and PIK3CA, yet rarely become cancerous. Mutations are therefore often necessary but not sufficient.

Second, many carcinogens do not act by mutating DNA. They act as promoters, typically through inflammation, which awakens pre-existing mutant clones. A well-known example is air pollution triggering lung tumors from dormant EGFR-mutant cells via interleukin-1β signalling.

Third, some tumors have few or no identifiable driver mutations, and experiments show that purely epigenetic disruption can initiate cancer.

Finally, context matters greatly: the tissue microenvironment, immune surveillance, aging, cell-of-origin state and cellular plasticity determine whether a mutant cell is suppressed, tolerated or expands.

Tumor initiation is thus now viewed as mutations plus permissive non-genetic conditions, reflected in updated "hallmarks of cancer" that include epigenetic reprogramming and phenotypic plasticity.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
The classic somatic mutation model held that accumulating DNA mutations in oncogenes and tumor suppressors directly triggers cancer. However, deep sequencing of healthy human tissues—including skin, esophagus, and blood—has revealed that normal aging cells routinely harbor hallmark cancer-driving mutations without ever forming tumors. Conversely, many known carcinogens do not mutate DNA at all, and certain cancers arise with remarkably few or even no detectable driver mutations.

These discoveries show that mutations alone are rarely sufficient to start a tumor; cellular and tissue context are equally decisive. Healthy tissue architecture and immune surveillance normally keep mutant clones dormant. Tumor initiation typically requires non-genetic "promoter" signals—such as chronic inflammation, tissue injury, infection, metabolic stress, or aging—that remodel the surrounding microenvironment and allow mutant cells to expand. At the same time, epigenetic reprogramming of DNA methylation and chromatin structure can silence protective genes and unlock stem-like plasticity, driving malignant behavior without new genetic changes. Cancer initiation is therefore now understood not merely as a genetic accident, but as an interplay between mutated cells, epigenetic state, and a permissive tissue ecosystem.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The classic "somatic mutation theory" says tumors begin when a cell gathers enough driver mutations in oncogenes and tumor suppressors. Several findings show that this is part of the story but not all of it.

First, healthy tissue is full of cancer-driver mutations. Deep sequencing of normal skin, esophagus, blood and other tissues found many clones carrying mutations in genes like TP53, NOTCH1 or KRAS, yet these clones almost never become cancer. So mutation alone usually isn't enough to start a tumor.

Second, some cancers have very few mutations. Many childhood tumors and some ependymomas seem to be driven mainly by epigenetic changes. Experiments in fruit flies showed that briefly disrupting Polycomb gene silencing can cause lasting tumors with no new DNA mutations.

Third, environmental "promoters" matter. In 2023, Swanton's group showed that air pollution drives lung cancer in people who never smoked. It does this by causing inflammation (IL-1β) that pushes existing EGFR-mutant cells to expand, not by causing new mutations.

So a tumor's start is now seen as mutations combined with epigenetic state, the cell's origin and identity, inflammation, aging, and the surrounding tissue environment.
